STEP 0 — DEEP RESEARCH FIRST (DO THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — MANDATORY)
Before writing a single word of narration or any image/video prompt, thoroughly RESEARCH the given Topic, Source Material, and Input/Canon Packet. Do not skip this. A shallow script produces a failed video.

Research silently (do not output your notes unless the template asks for a packet) and establish:

Verified core facts — what actually happened (or, for fiction: the locked rule, canon, and inputs supplied), who is involved, where and when. Separate confirmed fact from legend, regional retelling, popular myth, or unestablished canon.

The single strongest HOOK ANGLE — the most surprising, emotional, or high-stakes entry point a cold viewer would stop scrolling for.

The core EMOTION of this episode (one word) and the single PAYOFF the viewer gets at the end.

Visual opportunities — which 3–5 moments are inherently cinematic and what each looks like (era, location, costume/design, light, scale, aspect).

Uncertainties — anything the sources disagree on, or inputs that are missing. NEVER invent quotations, verses, dates, statistics, dialogue presented as factual, or canon you were not given. Omit unsupported specifics or qualify them briefly. For sequels, never pretend to remember unavailable episodes — ask for the canon or write a clearly standalone version.

Only after this research is solid, proceed to the workflow below. Source/canon fidelity over invention — but emotion and clarity over dry recitation.

PRODUCTION-LEVEL VISUAL STANDARD (MANDATORY FOR EVERY IMAGE PROMPT)
Every image_prompt must be a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade generation prompt of 70–120 words — never a one-line description. ONE-LINE or vague visual prompts are FORBIDDEN and count as a failed deliverable.

Each image prompt MUST cover:

Exact subject + story moment with full continuity descriptors repeated verbatim (never "same as before").

Readable pose, expression, and interaction matching its narration segment (using faceless/anonymous/environmental framing by default for real people).

Setting with era/materials, foreground/background depth, and scale.

Deliberate shot size + camera angle, varied every scene.

Lighting direction + time of day + palette + the episode's locked visual treatment.

Correct aspect composition (9:16 vertical) with key elements clear of caption/UI zones, legible on a phone.

A concise negative instruction inside the SAME prompt (no text/captions/logos/watermarks, no extra limbs, no duplicated subjects, no distorted faces, no style drift, no period-inappropriate objects).

BANNED: "Raft on ocean, cinematic light."

REQUIRED: Full shootable specifics a generator can render — what vehicle/gear, in what exact condition, doing what, where exactly, which light from which direction, which framing, which foreground/background layers, which mood.

HOOK EVERY TIME: The opening scene (and thumbnail/cover frame) must work as a scroll-stopper — an immediate physical predicament, dramatic silhouette, or decisive story instant with scale and depth. No channel intros, generic greetings, or summaries before the hook.

Self-check before returning: Count the words of EVERY image prompt (expand any under 70 words with concrete visual detail). Never pad with filler adjectives — add specifics the generator can render.

🧭 AGAINST THE ODDS — EXTRAORDINARY TRUE STORIES
MASTER PROMPT FILE (Merged) — Version 3.0 (Dynamic Tag Edition)
SHORT — IMAGE ONLY — Bible + Script Prompt + Production Prompt + Workflow Guide, with the Dynamic Tag System
A complete vertical survival story told with narration, still images, and text overlays. No generated video, animated image-to-video clips, stock video, or motion prompts.

🏷️ THE THREE-TAG MASTER PROTOCOL (Narration + Visuals + Motion Graphics / Metadata)
This pipeline enforces a strict THREE-TAG SYSTEM:

1. Audio Narration Tag: Exactly one <script>...</script> block housing the clean TTS-ready narration in Section 2B.

2. Dynamic Numbered Image Tags: Sequential <image_prompt0>, <image_prompt1>, <image_prompt2>, ... <image_prompt[N]> tags enclosing each self-contained still generation prompt in Section 3.
- Crucial Rule on <image_prompt0>: Index 0 is strictly reserved for the external promotional cover/thumbnail (16:9). It is never placed inside the video editing timeline.
- Story Stills: The actual narrative starts at <image_prompt1> and increments continuously through scene stills, the Follow Frame, and the End Card.

3. Dynamic Motion Graphics & Metadata Tags: Sequential <metadata1>, <metadata2>, ... <metadata[N]> tags specifying high-retention studio motion graphics (badges, counters, maps, reticles, headlines).
The AI decides where and when to trigger each motion graphic based on the story beats, but MUST include them where relevant:

Available Motion Graphic Archetypes for <metadata>:
- polaroid_badge: Use when introducing a person, survivor, rescuer, or critical location. Displays a photo cutout with 3D tilt and drifting motion over the scene. Must include an Asset Prompt for an isolated subject on clean background.
  Format:
  <metadata1>
  #scene 2
  Type: polaroid_badge
  Title: [Name / Place]
  Detail: [Role / Year / Location]
  Asset Prompt: [Self-contained prompt for an isolated photo cutout on clean background]
  </metadata1>

- telemetry_counter: Use whenever explicit numbers, statistics, altitudes, drop depths, survivor elapsed days, or speeds are spoken. Displays rapid odometer ticker count up (0 -> target).
  Format:
  <metadata2>
  #scene 4
  Type: telemetry_counter
  Target: [Integer numeral e.g. 24000]
  Unit: [FT / DAYS / MPH / KM]
  Label: [Short label e.g. CREVASSE DEPTH]
  Detail: [Context e.g. Freefall into ice abyss]
  </metadata2>

- route_map: Use for journeys, travel, evacuation paths, or flight lines between locations. Displays animated vector route line drawing with radar destination ping.
  Format:
  <metadata3>
  #scene 7
  Type: route_map
  Origin: [Departure place]
  Destination: [Arrival place]
  Distance: [Distance e.g. 130 KM or 80 MILES]
  Detail: [Route descriptor]
  </metadata3>

- newspaper_headline: Use for archival reports, investigation records, breaking news, or official declarations. Displays authentic newsprint card with animated yellow marker wipe.
  Format:
  <metadata4>
  #scene 9
  Type: newspaper_headline
  Publication: [Newspaper or Agency name]
  Headline: [Uppercase headline]
  Snippet: [Brief supporting sentence]
  Highlight: [Key words to highlight with yellow marker wipe]
  </metadata4>

- object_spotlight: Use to direct viewer focus to a critical physical item or piece of gear visible in the scene (e.g. cut rope, ice axe, compass). Displays pulsing targeting reticle and callout line.
  Format:
  <metadata5>
  #scene 11
  Type: object_spotlight
  Target: [Physical item visible in scene]
  Title: [Short title]
  Detail: [Material / spec / model]
  </metadata5>

- chapter_title: Use for major act breaks, turning points, or the story hook. Bold cinematic typography with accent tag.
  Format:
  <metadata6>
  #scene 1
  Type: chapter_title
  Title: [Chapter Headline]
  Tag: [ACT I / CHAPTER I / PROLOGUE]
  </metadata6>

LOCKED FORMAT: SHORT — IMAGE ONLY. RUNTIME: 45–75 seconds by default; up to 120 seconds when the selected duration requires it. The run request Target duration overrides this default. NARRATION: Simple English. ASPECT: 9:16 for playback; a separate optional 16:9 promotional thumbnail.

SOURCE FIRST: No invented facts, dialogue, people, countdowns, or rescue attempts.

RETENTION FIRST: Clear immediate stakes, consequential progress, useful intermediate payoffs, and a complete ending.

PART 3 — 🧭 SCRIPT PROMPT (Creative Pass — Run FIRST)
Your ONLY job is to turn supplied, verified content into an English script for review. Do not generate image prompts, motion prompts, thumbnails, or engagement packages in this pass.

⚙️ STEP 0 — CONTENT ANALYSIS (SILENT)
Identify content type, format, central predicament, verified outcome, primary emotion, chronology, people, locations, and source gaps.

🎯 HOOK RULES — STAKES + A SPECIFIC QUESTION
The first spoken line starts with the most compelling verified predicament, failed option or counterintuitive survival fact (4–10 words). Establish who faces what concrete danger in seconds 1–3 and why the obvious escape is unavailable by seconds 5–8. Prefer a direct factual statement that creates a question over a vague rhetorical question. Do not invent a countdown, private thought, quotation or rescue uncertainty. Keep the central question clear while giving an early concrete answer, clue or consequence in the next one or two sentences. Every following sentence must change what the viewer knows, what the protagonist can do, or what the choice will cost. Connect beats through cause and effect; cut repeated setup, biography before the predicament, redundant adjectives and generic suspense. Aim for a meaningful development about every 5–8 seconds where the story supports it, inside the existing scene structure; this is a writing guide, not a cut, scene-count or speech-speed requirement. Use short, natural spoken sentences, clear subjects and concrete verbs. Never hide basic context just to manufacture curiosity. Silently compare three different opening lines and use the clearest, most specific one that the story actually pays off; output only the chosen line in the existing format. Read the opening without the title: the viewer must understand the situation and have a specific reason to hear the next sentence. Remove any line that adds neither necessary context nor a new development. These are editorial choices, not guaranteed audience metrics.

The hook must be the first spoken line.

Never start with "Welcome back," channel introductions, or episode numbers.

🎯 MIDPOINT RE-HOOK RULE
Place one primary re-hook near 50–60% of the planned runtime based on a documented failed attempt, discovery or changed constraint (5–12 words). Explain specifically how it changes the next survival decision; do not repeat the danger or tease an unnamed surprise. Keep chronology and the distinction between what survivors and rescuers knew accurate. Resolve the opening promise with the actual outcome and the decisive reason, action or cost before any closing line. Place the strongest earned payoff in the final story beat, with useful smaller payoffs beforehand; never stretch an already answered question or hide a known outcome behind fake mystery. Finish on a concise consequence or an earlier detail whose meaning has changed, without recapping the story or adding a generic moral. A callback may reward replay only after the story is complete; no forced cliffhanger or missing answer. Preserve the existing CTA or blessing requirement and keep it brief, after resolution; add no extra engagement requests. No "wait until the end," "you won't believe," or empty "but then everything changed" lines.

### ⚖️ MANDATORY 50/50 MEDIA SPLIT (50% VIDEO / 50% IMAGE)
For every mixed script, you MUST enforce a strict 50% video and 50% still-image split:
- Alternating rhythm: Alternate media types across scenes with Scene 1 ALWAYS as a video to hook the user (Scene 1: Video, Scene 2: Image, Scene 3: Video, Scene 4: Image, etc.) so exactly 50% of the scenes are video and 50% are images.
- For an odd total number of scenes (e.g. 15 scenes), provide 8 videos and 7 images with Scene 1 as the opening hook video.
- Every video scene MUST have both an <image_prompt> (to generate the reference keyframe) and a <video_prompt> (for image-to-video animation).

STEP 0 — DEEP RESEARCH FIRST (DO THIS BEFORE ANYTHING ELSE — MANDATORY)
Before writing a single word of narration or any image/video prompt, thoroughly RESEARCH the given Topic, Source Material, and Input/Canon Packet. Do not skip this. A shallow or visually under-documented case produces a failed video.

Research silently (do not output raw notes unless the template asks for a packet) and establish:

Verified core facts — what actually happened, who was involved, where and when, what the person/group knew at each stage, what search/rescue teams knew, and the verified outcome. Separate VERIFIED, ATTRIBUTED, DISPUTED and UNKNOWN claims.

The strongest truthful hook angle — the most surprising, emotional or high-stakes source-backed fact that a cold viewer can understand immediately without a misleading countdown, fake mystery or invented quote.

The core emotion and payoff — choose one dominant emotion and one concrete factual payoff: how survival, escape, discovery or rescue became possible, or what the investigation established.

Visual opportunities — identify 5–8 moments that can be shown accurately: terrain, route, weather, object state, search area, shelter, vehicle, signal, map, rescue environment or aftermath. Mark whether each is ARCHIVE, MAP/DIAGRAM, ILLUSTRATIVE RECONSTRUCTION or EXTERNAL_REQUIRED.

Cross-model continuity facts — before prompting, collect only source-supported details that can safely stay identical across independently generated images and videos: person count, anonymity requirement, terrain geometry, object type/condition, weather by beat, time-of-day if known, camera-safe orientation, and any fixed colour/material information.

Uncertainties — list anything sources disagree on or do not establish. UNKNOWN means do not visualize a precise factual detail. Never convert an unknown into a convenient costume, facial feature, injury, weather event, vehicle model, time, route or rescue action merely for cinematic continuity.

Visual truth boundary — decide which moments can be reconstructed without pretending to show the exact historical frame. If the evidence supports only “they crossed rough terrain,” do not generate a precise cliff, rope technique or injury unless sourced.

Chronology compression check — identify any time jump or combined event required by the short runtime. Narration may compress exposition, but the visuals must not imply that events separated by hours or days occurred continuously.

Rights/disclosure check — separate factual verification from permission to use an asset. A source proving a fact does not automatically grant image/video rights.

Only after the evidence, visual truth boundary and continuity facts are solid, proceed to the workflow below. Source fidelity over spectacle; clarity and human stakes over dry recitation.

PRODUCTION-LEVEL VISUAL STANDARD (MANDATORY FOR EVERY IMAGE AND VIDEO PROMPT)
This template assumes the still-image generator and video generator may be completely different models with NO shared reference image, NO shared seed, NO shared latent state and NO memory of earlier outputs. Therefore consistency must come from a repeated text specification, not from phrases such as “same person,” “same location,” or “continue the previous shot.”

Every image_prompt must contain a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade prompt of roughly 160–240 words before its separate Negative Prompt and Style Tags. Every video_prompt must contain a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade prompt of roughly 220–320 words describing ONE continuous achievable shot. These are target ranges, not padding quotas: use concrete renderable information rather than decorative adjectives.

TEXT-ONLY CROSS-MODEL CONTINUITY SYSTEM — MANDATORY
Before Section 3, create a private episode continuity packet from the approved Bible. For every recurring element, write short canonical lock strings and copy them verbatim into every relevant image and video prompt:

VISUAL TREATMENT LOCK: documentary reconstruction style, realism level, contrast, texture, colour treatment, aspect ratio and disclosure character.

SUBJECT LOCK: only source-supported identifying facts; otherwise a deliberately non-identifying reconstruction rule such as face hidden, back view, distant silhouette or offscreen presence. Never invent facial identity to improve consistency.

LOCATION LOCK: stable terrain/layout facts, horizon/shore/cave/wall/road orientation, major materials, relative object placement and scale. Weather/time-of-day are locked per timeline beat, not globally.

🎯 HOOK RULES — STAKES + A SPECIFIC QUESTION
The first spoken line starts with a specific verified danger, failed option or counterintuitive survival fact (4–12 words), creating one question the episode will answer. Establish who faces what concrete danger in seconds 1–3 and why the obvious escape is unavailable by seconds 5–8. Prefer a clear factual statement over a vague rhetorical question. Do not invent a countdown, private thought, quotation or rescue uncertainty. Keep the central question clear while giving an early concrete answer, clue or consequence in the next one or two sentences. Every following sentence must change what the viewer knows, what the protagonist can do, or what the choice will cost. Connect beats through cause and effect; cut repeated setup, biography before the predicament, redundant adjectives and generic suspense. Aim for a meaningful development about every 5–8 seconds where the story supports it, inside the existing scene structure; this is a writing guide, not a cut, scene-count or speech-speed requirement. Use short, natural spoken sentences, clear subjects and concrete verbs. Never hide basic context just to manufacture curiosity. Silently compare three different opening lines and use the clearest, most specific one that the story actually pays off; output only the chosen line in the existing format. Read the opening without the title: the viewer must understand the situation and have a specific reason to hear the next sentence. Remove any line that adds neither necessary context nor a new development. These are editorial choices, not guaranteed audience metrics.

🎯 MIDPOINT RE-HOOK RULE
Place one primary re-hook near 45–65% of the planned runtime based on a documented failed attempt, discovery or changed constraint. Explain specifically how it changes the next survival decision; do not repeat the danger or tease an unnamed surprise. Keep chronology and the distinction between what survivors and rescuers knew accurate. Resolve the opening promise with the actual outcome and the decisive reason, action or cost before any closing line. Place the strongest earned payoff in the final story beat, with useful smaller payoffs beforehand; never stretch an already answered question or hide a known outcome behind fake mystery. Finish on a concise consequence or an earlier detail whose meaning has changed, without recapping the story or adding a generic moral. A callback may reward replay only after the story is complete; no forced cliffhanger or missing answer. Preserve the existing CTA or blessing requirement and keep it brief, after resolution; add no extra engagement requests. No "wait until the end," "you won't believe," or empty "but then everything changed" lines.

extractedScript:
In 1982, Steven Callahan’s sailboat sank in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean.

Eight hundred miles west of the Canary Islands,

a violent night storm and a catastrophic hull breach sent the twenty-one-foot sloop Napoleon Solo plunging into the dark abyss.

With mere seconds to react, Callahan scrambled into a tiny six-foot Avon life raft,

diving back into the flooding cabin to salvage a spear gun, navigation charts, and solar stills.

Drifting alone on endless ocean swells, he faced immediate dehydration under a blistering tropical sun.

Using his engineering background, Callahan operated portable solar stills,

blistered his hands distilling a pint of water a day,

and hunted raw mahi-mahi and flying fish to survive like an aquatic caveman.

Weeks blurred into months as aggressive sharks battered his thin

rubber hull and multiple passing cargo ships ignored his distress flares.

Constantly patching leaks just to stay afloat, Callahan tracked his grueling drift across eighteen hundred miles of open water.

Then, on day seventy-six, near the islands of the Caribbean,

local fishermen spotted a weathered orange raft and pulled a skeletal, sun-ravaged Callahan from the sea.

Weeks blurred into months as aggressive sharks battered his thin

rubber hull and multiple passing cargo ships ignored his distress flares.

Constantly patching leaks just to stay afloat, Callahan tracked his grueling drift across eighteen hundred miles of open water.

Then, on day seventy-six, near the islands of the Caribbean,

local fishermen spotted a weathered orange raft and pulled a skeletal, sun-ravaged Callahan from the sea.

# Research Dossier: Steven Callahan — 76 Days Adrift in an Atlantic Life Raft

## 1. Verified Facts, Background & Key Data
* **The Protagonist**: Steven Callahan (born February 6, 1952), an American author, naval architect, and experienced solo sailor.
* **The Vessel & Sinking**: Callahan designed and built his 21-foot fiberglass sloop, the *Napoleon Solo*. On January 29, 1982, he set sail from El Hierro in the Canary Islands, heading west toward Antigua. On February 5, 1982 (7 days out, roughly 800 miles west of the Canaries), a violent night storm and an impact with an unknown object (suspected to be a whale) stove a hole in the hull.
* **The Life Raft**: As the *Napoleon Solo* flooded, Callahan scrambled into a small, 6-person Avon inflatable life raft measuring roughly 6 feet across. Before the sloop went under, he made dangerous dives into the sinking cabin to retrieve essential survival items: a sleeping bag, a cushion, an emergency kit, signal flares, a spear gun, navigation charts, a copy of Dougal Robertson’s *Sea Survival* manual, and two solar stills for freshwater generation.
* **The Ordeal (76 Days)**: 
  * *Water*: Desalination was achieved via portable solar stills and catching rainwater, averaging roughly a pint of water a day. Operating the equipment severely blistered and tore his hands.
  * *Food*: He lived like an "aquatic caveman," spearing and eating mahi-mahi (dorado), triggerfish, flying fish, barnacles, and seabirds raw. 
  * *Setbacks*: Schools of mahi-mahi and circling sharks battered the raft. The fish frequently threatened to puncture his thin rubber flotation tubes, forcing constant emergency patching. He also missed multiple passing ships that failed to see his distress flares.
* **The Outcome**: After drifting approximately 1,800 nautical miles across the Atlantic, Callahan was spotted by local fishermen off the island of Marie-Galante (near Guadeloupe) on April 20, 1982—his 76th day adrift. He had lost nearly 40 pounds, suffering from severe salt sores and exhaustion, but survived. He documented his experience in the 1986 bestselling memoir *Adrift: Seventy-six Days Lost at Sea*.

---

## 2. Chronological Story Arc & Scene Beats (~90s)
* **Immediate Danger (Hook)**: Sinking in the black of night; a 21-foot sailboat flooding instantly after a catastrophic hull breach 800 miles from land.
* **Difficult Choices (Setup)**: Dives into the sinking cabin to salvage minimal survival tools—a 6-foot rubber life raft, a spear gun, and solar stills—just as the *Napoleon Solo* slips beneath the waves.
* **Escalation & Setbacks**: Weeks of open-ocean isolation. Dehydration, blistering sun, and aggressive schools of mahi-mahi and sharks physically puncturing and threatening his fragile raft. 
* **Decisive Action**: Using engineering know-how, Callahan builds solar stills to stave off fatal thirst, matches wits with sea predators to harvest raw food, and tracks his path toward shipping lanes.
* **Verified Outcome (Payoff)**: On day 76, near the Caribbean, local fishermen spot the weathered orange raft and pull a skeletal, sun-ravaged Callahan to safety, completing an epic 1,800-mile drift.

---

## 3. Visual & World-Building Canon
* **Setting & Era**: Early 1982; deep-water mid-Atlantic ocean, shifting from violent stormy night squalls to blistering, endless sun-baked horizon lines.
* **The Sinking Sloop**: A small white fiberglass sloop (*Napoleon Solo*) going down stern-first into dark, churning gray water.
* **The Life Raft**: A tiny, bright orange, 6-foot inflatable Avon rubber life raft with a spray canopy, battered by massive, heavy ocean swells.
* **Character Appearance (Steven Callahan)**: A young man in his early 30s with a rugged beard, salt-crusted skin, severe sunburn/blisters, wearing sun-bleached clothing that gradually becomes tattered as he drops nearly 40 pounds over the 76 days.
* **Props & Atmosphere**: Improvised spear gun, salt-encrusted solar still bags, raw fish strips drying, swarms of mahi-mahi (dorado) with iridescent blue/green scales flashing beneath dark water, and dorsal fins of sharks circling the perimeter.

---

## 4. Scriptwriter Directives
* **Factual Anchors**: Strictly reference the 76-day duration, the 1,800-mile drift distance, the 6-foot Avon life raft, and his location 800 miles west of the Canary Islands.
* **Key Terminology**: Use precise terms like *solar still*, *mahi-mahi*, *hull breach*, and *Avon life raft*.
* **Tone**: Gripping, visceral, and focused on human resilience and ingenuity against hostile nature. Do not sensationalize with fake details; the stark reality of solar desalination, raw fish protein, and structural raft repairs provides all the dramatic tension required.

Before writing a single word of narration or any image/video prompt, thoroughly RESEARCH the given Topic, Source Material, and Input/Canon Packet. Do not skip this. A shallow script produces a failed video.

Research silently (do not output your notes unless the template asks for a packet) and establish:

Verified core facts — what actually happened (or, for fiction: the locked rule, canon, and inputs supplied), who is involved, where and when. Separate confirmed fact from legend, regional retelling, popular myth, or unestablished canon.

The single strongest HOOK ANGLE — the most surprising, emotional, or high-stakes entry point a cold viewer would stop scrolling for.

The core EMOTION of this episode (one word) and the single PAYOFF the viewer gets at the end.

Visual opportunities — which 3–5 moments are inherently cinematic and what each looks like (era, location, costume/design, light, scale, aspect).

Uncertainties — anything the sources disagree on, or inputs that are missing. NEVER invent quotations, verses, dates, statistics, dialogue presented as factual, or canon you were not given. Omit unsupported specifics or qualify them briefly. For sequels, never pretend to remember unavailable episodes — ask for the canon or write a clearly standalone version.

Only after this research is solid, proceed to the workflow below. Source/canon fidelity over invention — but emotion and clarity over dry recitation.

PRODUCTION-LEVEL VISUAL STANDARD (MANDATORY FOR EVERY IMAGE PROMPT)
Every image_prompt must be a DETAILED, self-contained, production-grade generation prompt of 70–120 words — never a one-line description. ONE-LINE or vague visual prompts are FORBIDDEN and count as a failed deliverable.

Each image prompt MUST cover:

Exact subject + story moment with full continuity descriptors repeated verbatim (never "same as before").

Readable pose, expression, and interaction matching its narration segment (using faceless/anonymous/environmental framing by default for real people).

Setting with era/materials, foreground/background depth, and scale.

Deliberate shot size + camera angle, varied every scene.

Lighting direction + time of day + palette + the episode's locked visual treatment.

Correct aspect composition (9:16 vertical) with key elements clear of caption/UI zones, legible on a phone.

A concise negative instruction inside the SAME prompt (no text/captions/logos/watermarks, no extra limbs, no duplicated subjects, no distorted faces, no style drift, no period-inappropriate objects).

BANNED: "Raft on ocean, cinematic light."

REQUIRED: Full shootable specifics a generator can render — what vehicle/gear, in what exact condition, doing what, where exactly, which light from which direction, which framing, which foreground/background layers, which mood.

HOOK EVERY TIME: The opening scene (and thumbnail/cover frame) must work as a scroll-stopper — an immediate physical predicament, dramatic silhouette, or decisive story instant with scale and depth. No channel intros, generic greetings, or summaries before the hook.

Identify content type, format, central predicament, verified outcome, primary emotion, chronology, people, locations, and source gaps.

🎯 HOOK RULES — STAKES + A SPECIFIC QUESTION
The first spoken line starts with the most compelling verified predicament, failed option or counterintuitive survival fact (4–10 words). Establish who faces what concrete danger in seconds 1–3 and why the obvious escape is unavailable by seconds 5–8. Prefer a direct factual statement that creates a question over a vague rhetorical question. Do not invent a countdown, private thought, quotation or rescue uncertainty. Keep the central question clear while giving an early concrete answer, clue or consequence in the next one or two sentences. Every following sentence must change what the viewer knows, what the protagonist can do, or what the choice will cost. Connect beats through cause and effect; cut repeated setup, biography before the predicament, redundant adjectives and generic suspense. Aim for a meaningful development about every 5–8 seconds where the story supports it, inside the existing scene structure; this is a writing guide, not a cut, scene-count or speech-speed requirement. Use short, natural spoken sentences, clear subjects and concrete verbs. Never hide basic context just to manufacture curiosity. Silently compare three different opening lines and use the clearest, most specific one that the story actually pays off; output only the chosen line in the existing format. Read the opening without the title: the viewer must understand the situation and have a specific reason to hear the next sentence. Remove any line that adds neither necessary context nor a new development. These are editorial choices, not guaranteed audience metrics.

The hook must be the first spoken line.

Never start with "Welcome back," channel introductions, or episode numbers.

Keep chronology and the distinction between what survivors and rescuers knew accurate. Resolve the opening promise with the actual outcome and the decisive reason, action or cost before any closing line. Place the strongest earned payoff in the final story beat, with useful smaller payoffs beforehand; never stretch an already answered question or hide a known outcome behind fake mystery. Finish on a concise consequence or an earlier detail whose meaning has changed, without recapping the story or adding a generic moral. A callback may reward replay only after the story is complete; no forced cliffhanger or missing answer.
